title: The Week That Was
gist: Lawfare's weekly roundup (Sept. 19, 2026) spans a nonkinetic playbook for forcing Iran to reopen the closed Strait of Hormuz, AfD gains in Germany, a CJEU ruling stripping liability exemptions from algorithmic platforms, gaps in EU and US state AI regulation, and administration efforts to cast doubt on US election integrity.

insights.claim: Lawfare contributor Liron Libman argued that nonkinetic countermeasures, rather than military force, could push Iran to reopen the closed Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Signals the Strait of Hormuz closure is a live, ongoing disruption; a nonkinetic policy path implies a slower reopening timeline for oil and shipping flows.
insights.locator: Liron Libman argued that nonkinetic countermeasures

insights.claim: Proposed nonkinetic options against Iran include restricting free passage of Iranian-flagged vessels and UN Security Council action to force compliance with international law.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Watch for reciprocal shipping restrictions on Iranian-flagged tankers and UNSC moves as catalysts for Hormuz reopening and tanker rates.
insights.quote: limits on the free passage of Iranian-flagged vessels or UN Security Council action
insights.locator: Libman explained potential options for affected states

themes.theme: Europe: far right, NATO flank, CJEU

insights.claim: The far-right Alternative für Deutschland is making a strong showing in German state elections, alarming the pro-democracy community about implications for Germany, Europe and the United States.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Rising AfD strength is a German political-risk factor for Bund spreads, EU cohesion and European defense/fiscal policy.
insights.locator: On Lawfare Daily, Orpett sat down with Constanze Stelzenmüller

insights.claim: Russian provocations in and near NATO territory related to Ukraine were among the week's major national security stories.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Ongoing Russia-NATO friction supports the European defense spending thesis and keeps an escalation tail risk priced.
insights.locator: On Rational Security, Scott Anderson sat down

insights.claim: A Court of Justice of the European Union ruling, arising from a French driving-assistance app barred from showing police checkpoints, removes the liability exemption for platforms that use algorithms to curate or prioritize user content.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
entities: Court of Justice of the European Union
insights.so_what: Algorithmically curated platforms in the EU face expanded liability for illegal user content, raising compliance and legal costs for social media and app platforms.
insights.quote: removes the exemption that platforms using algorithms to curate or prioritize user content previously held from liability
insights.locator: Michael FitzGerald explored a Court of Justice

insights.claim: Eliška Andrš argued the EU AI Act likely still covers most internally used AI models that never reach the market, despite research-and-development exceptions, subjecting them to premarket enforcement.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frontier labs and enterprises running internal AI in the EU may face compliance obligations they assumed were exempt.
insights.quote: most internal AI models may ultimately still be covered by premarket enforcement
insights.locator: Eliška Andrš examined whether the European Union

insights.claim: New state mandatory AI safety incident reporting laws in California, Illinois and New York do not specify what happens after an incident is reported, leaving an investigative gap.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A state-level AI incident regime is forming; expect follow-on rules requiring data preservation and dedicated investigative teams, adding compliance cost for AI labs.
insights.quote: They do not clarify what happens after an incident is reported
insights.locator: Christopher David LaRoche highlighted an important gap

insights.claim: Proposed fixes for AI incident investigations include requiring labs to preserve incident data and creating dedicated teams to assist investigators, since existing investigative powers fit AI forensics poorly.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Forensic data-retention mandates would add logging/storage and governance obligations for frontier AI companies.
insights.locator: To address the gap, he suggested regulators

insights.claim: Kenji Yoshino argues AI oversight should use independent overseers, external standards and transparent decisions, modeled on lessons from Meta's Oversight Board.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: An Oversight Board-style governance model could become a template or pressure point for frontier AI companies' self-regulation.
insights.locator: On Scaling Laws, Frazier and Kate Klonick

insights.claim: Turmoil hit the tech world after a former Anthropic researcher urged the AI industry to slow down.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Internal dissent at frontier labs can shift sentiment and regulatory momentum around AI development pace.
insights.locator: On Rational Security, Scott Anderson sat down

insights.claim: Experts leaving academia for the AI industry and students joining AI firms instead of pursuing further study create a dual brain drain that erodes the independent expertise needed to regulate and understand AI.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Talent concentration in AI labs strengthens incumbents' moat but raises the odds of policy intervention to fund independent AI research.
insights.locator: Bharat Chandar and Frazier warned about the dual brain drain

insights.claim: Marcel Anduiza argued Latin America's Treaty of Tlatelolco shows prohibition-based approaches can be viable as nuclear powers weigh integrating AI into nuclear command, control and communications.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: AI in nuclear C3 is emerging as an arms-control topic; watch for treaty-style limits affecting defense-AI contractors.
insights.locator: Marcel Anduiza explained what lessons can be learned

insights.claim: Julia Curlee argued Trump administration claims of Chinese election interference and voting-machine vulnerability are part of efforts to manipulate intelligence that could later justify blocking unwelcome election results.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Raises US political tail risk around contested election outcomes; watch for voting-machine vendor and election-certification disputes.
insights.locator: Curlee argued that the Trump administration’s recent claims

insights.claim: The Supreme Court refused to stay the injunction against President Trump's executive order targeting mail voting, while litigation continues over the use of SAVE data for elections.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Courts are still checking executive election actions, a key input for assessing institutional stability risk.

insights.claim: Jack Goldsmith argued the 2001 AUMF is obsolete because expanded Article II presidential authority has eroded its practical need, so only Congress can meaningfully rein in presidential war powers.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Unilateral presidential war-making faces few legal constraints, raising the probability of sudden US military actions (e.g., in the Middle East) without congressional approval.
insights.locator: Jack Goldsmith asserted that the 2001 Authorization

insights.claim: Cindy Cohn and Bruce Schneier argued 25 years of expanding post-9/11 mass surveillance, increasingly by private companies, is harmful and legally unsound, and Congress should consider comprehensive privacy-law changes.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Comprehensive federal privacy legislation would hit ad-tech and data-broker business models.
insights.locator: Cindy Cohn and Bruce Schneier weighed the costs

insights.claim: The US military disabled ad identifiers to prevent service members from being tracked, while a dark web service was found selling access to identification documents such as US driver's licenses.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Institutional moves against ad-ID tracking signal growing security framing of ad-tech data, a regulatory headwind for data brokers.
insights.locator: In the latest edition of the Seriously Risky Business

insights.claim: Daniel Byman argued US officials treated 9/11 as a harbinger of worse attacks when it was exceptional, underestimated how sustained counterterrorism pressure diminished the threat, and overestimated US ability to reshape Middle East politics.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A reminder to discount worst-case terrorism scenarios and nation-building ambitions when pricing geopolitical risk.
insights.locator: Daniel Byman identified five analytic mistakes

insights.claim: Without a comprehensive plan, repeat terrorist attacks by recidivists are likely, and prevention efforts can inadvertently reinforce the social isolation that deepens extremist commitment.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Security-risk models should account for recidivism as a persistent source of attacks.
insights.locator: Peter Beck, Seamus Hughes, and Camden Carmichael
